articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

paras.en: The brainâs hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

- A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."
How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear
To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.
Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger
Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.
A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD
The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.
The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.
The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

articles.title: The Star Wars Eclipse — Want to see the 2027 total solar eclipse on Tatooine? Head to Tunisia
articles.author: Jamie Carter

paras.en: On Aug. 2, 2027, darkness will fall on Tatooine. The path of the "eclipse of the century" crosses southern Tunisia, putting several of the most famous Star Wars filming locations in the moon's shadow for up to four minutes. Around Tozeur, eclipse chasers can experience totality among the dunes of Mos Espa and the rocky Jundland Wastes, while on Djerba, locations used for Mos Eisley and Obi-Wan Kenobi's home will also briefly go dark.

Other iconic sites are tantalizingly close to — but beyond — the southern edge of the path of totality. For example, Hotel Sidi Idriss, used as Lars Homestead in the original movie and in Attack of the Clones, gets only a 99.98% partial eclipse. So too Chott el-Djerid, site of the famous "binary" sunset over the salt flats — let's hope someone gets a partial eclipse shot from this iconic site. The nearby real-life Tunisian town of Tataouine is also just outside of the path.

For Star Wars fans planning to chase the 2027 eclipse, location will be everything. Here are four filming locations firmly inside the path of totality. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.
Location: south of Chott el-Gharsa, Tozeur Governorate, southwest Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 9 seconds

With a massive budget and three prequels to make, Lucasfilm built a new film set that would double as the Mos Espa spaceport on Tatooine for The Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones. This is where Qui-Gon Jinn, Obi-Wan Kenobi, Jar Jar Binks and Padme get stranded, where they meet Anakin Skywalker and where the podrace takes place. Now abandoned, it's in the middle of nowhere, between two huge salt lakes and subject to the intense heat and moving Eriguet dunes — but it is firmly within the path of totality. Nearby are two other shooting locations — the Ong Jemel outcrop, where Darth Maul arrives on the scene, and Yardang, where Qui-Gon and Darth Maul battle — the first-ever lightsaber duel filmed on location.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Location: Jebel Sidi Bouhlel canyon, Dghoumès National Park, Tozeur, southwest Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 37 seconds

Often called "Star Wars Canyon" by fans and crew, Maguer Gorge in Jebel Sidi Bouhlel doubled as the Jundland Wastes of Tatooine in Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope. It's where Luke Skywalker is attacked by Tusken Raiders, where Obi-Wan Kenobi first appears and where Luke and Obi-Wan discover the slaughtered Jawas. The canyon also provided the distant view of Mos Eisley — the famous "wretched hive of scum and villainy." On Aug. 2, 2027, you'll likely be pointing your macrobinoculars at the eclipsed sun rather than Tusken Raiders.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Steven Spielberg later filmed here for Raiders of the Lost Ark, including the scene in which Indiana Jones threatens to destroy the Ark with a bazooka. Just south of Dghoumès National Park is a desert oasis called Bouhlel Sdada, used for the archaeological dig scenes in Raiders.
Location: Ajim city center, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:10 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 55 seconds

Djerba Island's palm trees, beaches and Mediterranean horizons will make it a popular destination for eclipse chasers after a long totality away from the heat and crowds of Luxor in Egypt. It's also home to three notable Star Wars filming locations. The original movie's Mos Eisley footage was shot here, with Ajim doubling as a Stormtrooper checkpoint ("These are not the droids you're looking for"), the Cantina exterior, and an alley near Docking Bay 94 where stormtroopers watch the Millennium Falcon blast off. In reality, it's an abandoned bakery.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: 4. Amghar Mosque (Obi-Wan Kenobi's house)
Location: Ajim outskirts, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes

Just north of Ajim, this mosque — originally a fisherman's house — was used as a stand-in for "Old Ben's" house, where Obi-Wan Kenobi gives Luke Skywalker a lightsaber. It was used purely for photography, and no actors set foot here. It was also cut from the movie's Special Edition in 1997, so you'll only find it in the original version. Completists might also want to check out Sidi Jemour Mosque to the north, which was used for scenes with Biggs Darklighter that didn't even make the final cut. IYKYK …

Tunisia's Star Wars locations are spread across the south, so the easiest way to see several is on an organized tour or with a private driver and guide. Where else to watch the eclipse in Tunisia

Tunisia is surely one of the most attractive destinations for the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse. Historical cloud cover is exceptionally low, while totality reaches around five and a half minutes near the centerline. It also offers established tourism infrastructure and generally lower August temperatures than Egypt, making it an obvious alternative for eclipse chasers hoping to avoid the biggest crowds around Luxor.

You can, of course, visit the Star Wars sets in the days before or after the eclipse. For Tunisia's maximum duration of totality, consider Sfax, where darkness lasts 5 minutes, 41 seconds, or nearby Chaffar Beach, with its long, open Mediterranean coastline. Offshore, the low-lying Kerkennah Islands get around 5 minutes, 39 seconds. Inland, Sidi Bouzid offers about 5 minutes, 33 seconds beneath typically dry skies, while the spectacular Roman amphitheater at El Jem gets 4 minutes, 23 seconds. On Djerba Island, meanwhile, beaches and extensive resort infrastructure make combining an eclipse chase with a conventional Mediterranean vacation particularly easy — with a view of Mos Eisley thrown in for good measure.

articles.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
articles.author: Robert Lea

paras.en: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.

The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats.

The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old. That means it is still host to collisions between planetary bodies similar to the ones that rocked the solar system during its infancy.

The team behind this research gained new insights into the Cat's Tail using 14 years of observations. This allowed them to solve the long-standing mystery of the violent conditions under which it formed.

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies — think something like Pluto," team leader Arin Avsar of the University of Arizona said in a statement. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."
Cosmic cat tail is also pleasingly fluffy

Comparing Beta Pictoris and our solar system, one thing rapidly becomes apparent: our cosmic neighborhood is relatively well-ordered. The planets orbit the sun with most space rocks neatly delegated into bands: the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt out beyond the orbit of Neptune.

However, this is a stark contrast to the solar system's violent and chaotic youth. Back then, the solar system was host to an infant star surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust in which collisions between bodies called planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — were commonplace.

Astronomers can't look back to the solar system's infancy, so to learn more about how our cosmic backyard took shape, they study nearby young planetary systems. Systems like Beta Pictoris. That doesn't mean it has been quick to divulge its secrets, though.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

This new study revealed that the feline feature is cat-like in more ways than just its shape. It's also pleasingly fluffy, Hubble observations suggest. That's because the grains that compose it are extremely porous.
"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," team member Kevin Wagner of the U of A said.

The scientists also discovered a hitherto undiscovered feature in the Cat's Tail — a warp that seems to be the result of an interaction between the trail of material and one of the planets in the system, Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant planet 10 times more massive than Jupiter.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units [one astronomical unit being the distance between Earth and the sun]."
The team's research was published last month in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. articles.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
articles.author: Andrew Jones

paras.en: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.

Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.

Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.
For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

articles.title: DETUMBLER: Airbus’ Passive Spin Stabilization Solution
articles.author: Airbus

paras.en: The tumbling crisis: why dead satellites threaten orbit

Every year, hundreds of satellites reach end-of-life, most are deorbited, but some fail abruptly. Yet, even when properly decommissioned, some dead satellites may start tumbling on their own, through the accumulation of tiny disturbances like solar radiation pressure, to the point where they become impossible to capture by active debris removal missions.

With over 36,500 tracked debris objects in orbit, the risk of cascading collisions is real. ESA warns that without ADR (Active Debris Removal) solutions, some LEO orbits will become unusable. Ensuring that all dead satellites are properly detumbled would be a major element towards making ADR economically feasible.
Detumbler: the game-changing alternative

Developed by Airbus R&D, the Detumbler is a passive magnetic damping device that stabilizes tumbling satellites before they become uncontrollable. Acting like an induction brake, it dissipates kinetic energy through the Earth’s magnetic field, stopping tumbling in a few months. For the first time, operators have a reliable, low-cost, fully passive solution to prevent post-mission tumbling.

Without power and thus actuators, the only phenomenon that can limit tumbling rates in a dead spacecraft are the natural eddy currents created by the Earth’s magnetic field in the satellite’s rotating metallic structure. Short circuiting the magnetorquers at the end of life could help boost that natural effect. Unfortunately, the resulting resistive torque is proportional to the low magnetic field squared (the induced dipole moment M is proportional to B, and the resulting magnetic torque is MxB), making such effects extremely weak, too weak to prevent spontaneous tumbling in case of any asymmetry in the external disturbances. As an example, in 2017, 12 years after decommissioning, Topex-Poseidon had reached a spin rate of 34 deg/s (40,000 Nms of accumulated momentum).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Despite its very modest mass and volume, the Detumbler can reach efficiencies many orders of magnitude higher, by using permanent magnets so that the braking torque is proportional to B, not B².

ESA’s Space Safety Program requires detumbling capacities for LEO missions >500kg (1100 lbs), targeting detumbling performances from 3°/s to 0.75°/s in less than a year. Airbus’ Detumbler is a leading solution for meeting ESA’s requirements and thus enabling active debris removal (ADR).
How the Detumbler works: a satellite’s “magnetic brake”

The magnetized rotor inside the Detumbler tends to remain aligned with the Earth’s magnetic field. As the satellite tumbles, the Detumbler’s conductive housing rotates around the magnetized rotor, thus causing magnetic braking through eddy currents. This slowly but steadily dissipates the satellite’s kinetic energy, reducing the angular momentum exponentially, ultimately reaching a detumbled steady-state with very low residual rates. This is achieved without the need for any electrical or computing power, contrary to all other attitude control actuators.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Detumbler can then cancel or respectively prevent tumbling in all situations that might cause it:
- catastrophic dynamic events (leaks, propulsion failures, impacts from debris or micrometeoroids)
- slow buildup of angular momentum through the relentless action of tiny disturbance sources such as asymmetric solar radiation pressure (similar to the YORP effect in astronomy).

Weighing around 200g (0,440 lbs), the palm-sized device can be integrated almost anywhere (just not too close to the magnetometer) into existing platform designs, with little-to-no modifications, making it an easy decision for future LEO space missions.
Detumbler is no longer in R&D, it’s TRL 8 and already commercially available through the Airbus Space Electronics product portfolio.
✔ 100% passive: Neither power nor attitude-control actuators intervention; working even after the end of the mission
✔ Compatible with a large range of platform sizes (from ~150 kg (330 lbs) to ~1.5 tons (3300 lbs)
✔ Detumbling within weeks for the smaller platforms, within a year for the upper end of the size range
✔ Prevents tumbling despite average external disturbances up to 5 µNm
✔ Tested under launch vibrations and orbital conditions.

While available now, Detumbler’s potential lies in large-scale adoption. MDA Space has selected the Detumbler for its first MDA AURORATM LEO satellite constellation order, with a view to tangibly ensuring a safer, sustainable use of Space. When the constellation launches, it will mark the first commercial large-scale integration of passive detumbling in orbit.

Detumbler is more than a product; it’s a cornerstone of Airbus’ sustainable space vision. By enabling active debris removal, it supports ESA’s Zero Debris targets and EU Space Traffic Management regulations, ensuring long-term orbital viability.

For Airbus, Detumbler proves that even the most complex space challenges can be solved through innovation and responsibility. As mega-constellations expand, technologies like Detumbler will be essential to preserving the usability of the shared low Earth orbit environment.
The Detumbler effect: stability for a sustainable future

The problem of tumbling satellites has persisted for decades, but Detumbler, ESA’s mandates, and renewed urgency for sustainability now require industry to solve it. By stabilizing uncontrolled satellites, Detumbler reduces ADR risks, costs, and complexity, making removal feasible at scale.
For operators, the message is clear: integrating Detumbler is not just compliance, it’s a business imperative. For the industry, it’s a step toward a stable and accessible orbit.

paras.en: Czech company Spacemanic and Belgian optical leader Simera Sense are teaming up to deliver a new dual-use satellite solution that can compete with bigger and heavier satellites. Simera Sense xScape200 Dual-Use (DU) camera is integrated into Spacemanic 16U CubeSat platform, bringing high-resolution imaging capabilities to a lightweight, compact spacecraft designed for repeatable deployment and constellation growth.

The xScape200 DU combines a compact 12U form factor, low SWaP, and standardised integration to give commercial and defence organisations high-resolution, dual-use imaging capabilities without the need for a larger spacecraft, increased launch costs, or power-intensive mission architectures.

Spacemanic designs and builds its satellite platforms, core subsystems and deployers in-house. Owning the whole chain lets the company shape the satellite around the camera instead of forcing the camera into a standard form factor. That covers the satellite’s structure and envelope, its mechanical, electrical, thermal and data interfaces, and how the satellite integrates with the deployer.

The SPACE CANNON deployer accommodates CubeSats up to 16U, with an expanded integration envelope for payloads with protruding elements on the sides and a tuna can at the bottom. This additional space supports larger payload configurations such as the xScape200 DU camera. Removable side panels on all four sides provide direct access to the satellite after integration, enabling final adjustments right before launch. SPACE CANNON is designed for integration with launch vehicles including Falcon 9, Ariane 6, Vega-C, HyImpulse SL1, InnoSpace Hanbit, Spectrum by Isar Aerospace, RFA ONE and HyPrSpace Baguette One.

articles.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA

paras.en: Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon
Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1's light-day milestone, and watch November's supermoon.
- Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs
- Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions
- Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise
- Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation
- Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions
- Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons
A month of meteor showers ... a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter ... and a supermoon!
November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky!
The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th.
Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate.
Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile.

Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer.
To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can.
Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together.
They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby.
Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side.
Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together - and then go their separate ways.
This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft - and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it!
If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer.
And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager.
On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon.
Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes. When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average - though the difference can be subtle.
This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January.
Look east around sunset to watch it rise. It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon.

articles.title: TB 26-10 Printed Circuit Board Assembly Chip Resistor Body Cracking
articles.author: Meagan Chappell

paras.en: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov.

Chip resistors are widely used in NASA projects, yet cases of alumina substrate cracking during environmental testing are rare. Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration, with fractures occurring across the short axis due to bending. Failure analyses ruled out defective lots and fatigue, identifying board flexure, component orientation, excessive solder, and mounting stresses as contributing factors. The bulletin recommends careful component placement, finite element analysis, controlled solder fillet height, thorough inspection, and functional thermal shock testing to mitigate flexure-induced cracking risks in ceramic body components on printed circuit boards.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The NESC noted historical lack of reported cases of chip resistors’ alumina substrate cracking during vibration and thermal cycling, although chip resistors are ubiquitous across NASA projects. Two instances of thick film chip resistor body cracking were observed during environmental acceptance testing on printed circuit board assemblies. Both failures occurred during thermal cycling after vibration testing, exhibiting intermittent open circuit failures at hot dwell temperatures that recovered at room temperature. Transverse fracture occurred at the mid-span of each resistor, running parallel to the terminations. The two resistors were installed in similar locations near the edge of the boards on two identical boards. Cracks in failed resistors were along the short axis of the resistor due to apparent bending of the resistors, Figure 1. Resistors showed no signs of pre-existing defects.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Causal Relationships Initial theories pointed to vibration-induced damage of potentially defective resistors since both resistors came from the same production lot. However, the resistor lot not only meets the requirements of procurement specification MIL-PRF-55342 but additional tests were performed and did not reveal any direct evidence of a defective resistor lot. There was no evidence of an elevated risk of defective resistors within the production lot.

Independent failure analyses concluded that the cracked chip resistors were due to bending/tensile failures. There was no clear-cut root cause or visible defect identifying a crack initiation site. Both resistors exhibited a single, straight crack across the short axis (perpendicular to the long axis), indicating a bending/tensile failure without twisting.

The damage signatures are not consistent with cyclic fatigue, likely ruling out fatigue failure during vibration. In addition, NESC independent optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Figure 2, of both resistors did not identify any clear flaw locations for fatigue damage initiation and progression; therefore, the possibility of defective resistors as well as fatigue vibration as the root cause becomes unlikely.

No direct root cause was identified, but contributing factors leading to increased design consideration needed for large footprint ceramic components located near the edges of a printed circuit board that can lead to stress cracks due to manufacturing or installation bow/twist of the printed circuit board include:

- Location of the relatively large resistors (case size 2512) next to the edge of the board with resistor’s long axis parallel to the card edge, increasing susceptibility to board flexure-induced damage.
- Excessive solder that extended to the top pads on the resistor terminations.
- Excessive bending moments or loads resulting from board bow/twist.
- Hard mounting the board to a rigid frame, which can store and amplify these bow/twist stresses.
- Suboptimal fastener torquing patterns, which may concentrate mounting stresses specifically at the resistor locations.
Guidelines for Assembly of Ceramic Body Components to Printed Circuit Boards
The following guidelines are to be considered given the recent experience.

- Component Orientation: Avoid orienting the long axis of large footprint ceramic components parallel to nearby printed circuit board edges to reduce susceptibility to global and local flexure damage.
- Finite Element Analysis: Perform sufficient Finite Element Analysis to demonstrate adequate stress and displacement margins on large components when they must be placed near the edge of the board.

- Solder Joint Fillet Limits: Keep solder off the top surface of terminations. Solder on top creates a rigid joint that transfers printed circuit board flexure directly into the ceramic increasing risk of flexure-induced cracking. Consult the individual parts manufacturers for guidance, as they may place specific limits on solder fillet height.

- Solder Joint Inspection: Inspect physical solder joints or review photographic images of the joints to verify that components have sufficient, but not excessive, solder fillets according to manufacturer limits.
- Functional Thermal Shock Testing: Perform one to three thermal cycles, including a hot-dwell functional test, prior to vibration testing, to document as built component integrity.
1. MIL-PRF-55342 Resistor, Chip, Fixed, Film, Nonestablished Reliability, Established Reliability, Space Level
2. MIL-PRF-55342/9 Resistor, Fixed, Film, Chip, Nonestablished Reliability, Established Reliability, Space Level, Style RM2512

articles.title: COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature

paras.en: COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
Agreement was formalised through the Yerevan Pathway as the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) closed in the Armenian capital on Saturday.
It sets out priorities for the four years left to deliver the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
“We cannot protect nature while continuing to finance its destruction,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
The pathway calls on countries to tackle subsidies that harm nature and to increase financial, scientific and technical support for developing countries.
It also calls for national budgets and economic decisions to be aligned with the framework, and for stronger monitoring and reporting.
“Over these two weeks we have demonstrated that differences can be bridged, commitments can become decisions and cooperation can deliver,” said COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Parties adopted nearly 50 decisions, covering areas including protected areas and forests, wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, and synthetic biology.
After intensive negotiations, they also agreed the Sevan Guidelines.
These set the rules of operation for a new permanent body strengthening the role of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in shaping global biodiversity policy.

Nearly $2 billion in new biodiversity funding was announced. This included $560 million under the Global Environment Facility’s latest replenishment and $500 million through the Species Recovery Alliance.
Another $330 million is going to the Value Nature Fund, which aims to mobilise private capital for nature.
Other initiatives included a new biodiversity bond and investment incubator launched by the Asian Development Bank, and new indicators to improve biodiversity monitoring and accountability.
“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
“Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet.”
The next conference, COP18, will be held in Ecuador, with two years remaining to achieve the targets.
“Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home,” said Ms. Schomaker.

articles.title: Air raid alerts and attacks on schools: the devastating face of education in Ukraine

paras.en: Air raid alerts and attacks on schools: the devastating face of education in Ukraine

Ukraine has sustained almost 2,000 attacks on education since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with some 270 this year alone, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Tuesday, a day after a strike at a school being used to distribute aid.

Since the start of the academic year, “children have experienced an average of 34 hours of air raid alarms during school time, equivalent to more than 13 per cent of scheduled learning” up to 20 October, with some regions impacted by 60-plus hours of alerts, said UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires.
Meanwhile, the UN's top aid official in Ukraine condemned Monday's attack on a school and shelter in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia region, that reportedly killed at least 29 civilians.

The majority of the victims were residents "who came to get aid at a local school and employees of the local administration", said Matthias Schmale, Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ukraine. "Subsequent strikes at the same location killed two rescuers and four police staff who responded to the first attack," he continued, noting that nearly 50 people are still missing.

In Kyiv, aid raid alarms increased from 12 in September 2025 to 71 in September 2026. In Dnipropetrovsk, Kirovohrad and Kharkiv regions, children have experienced more than 60 hours of school-time alarms. This is equivalent to approximately one quarter of scheduled learning hours, affecting more than 560,000 children.

“I’ve just returned to in-person school; however, we still spend most of our school day in a shelter because of air raids,” said 15-year-old Katia from the Mykolaiv region, whose testimony Mr. Pires shared.

He reiterated the visible mental health toll that the war continues to have on all Ukrainian children, recalling his visit a month ago where he talked to youngsters who have to learn underground “because it’s not safe for them to be above ground”.

Despite the relative safety afforded by the classroom bunkers, “even then, they are dealing with air raid alarms all the time (and) you could feel that some of them, especially the older ones, expressed a lot of anxiety and shared with us their inability to fully concentrate and kind of leave what’s happening above ground.”

Echoing those concerns, the head of the UN global fund Education Cannot Wait, Maysa Jabout, explained that the “huge impact” of war everywhere on children has forced it to prioritise funding for psychosocial counselling, “carving away … “essential money that we need for teaching and learning in order to support children’s ability to cope with learning in very difficult circumstances”.

articles.title: Gender equality pays off for business – so why are companies pulling back?

paras.en: Gender equality pays off for business – so why are companies pulling back?
The recommendation comes from the International Labour Organization (ILO) in its report Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success, published on Tuesday.
Between 2013 and 2025, the share of companies with a woman board chair rose from 13.1 per cent to 30.1 per cent. The share with a woman CEO climbed from 23.5 per cent to 28.2 per cent.

Yet women remain under-represented in management overall, occupying around a third of managerial-level roles. Gender balance increased at senior and top management levels during the same period but declined at junior and middle management.
The report draws on a 2025 ILO survey of 11,957 enterprises in 99 countries, as well as surveys conducted in 2013 and 2018, 30 years of labour market data, secondary research and case studies.
Nearly 70 per cent of enterprises surveyed in 2025 said gender equality and diversity initiatives had improved business outcomes, up more than 11 percentage points from 2018.

Among those reporting increased profits through initiatives promoting women in management, 87.4 per cent reported gains of at least five per cent. Firms with women CEOs and board chairs were also more likely to report better business outcomes.

Still, although nearly three quarters (74.8 per cent) of enterprises reported having a gender equality and diversity policy or equivalent in place in 2025, the share that implemented them stood at 26.5 per cent, down from 37.4 per cent in 2018.
“The decline included measures that enterprises themselves identified as among the most effective, including maternity leave and support programmes and equal pay initiatives,” the ILO said.
The UN agency noted that the findings come despite major advances in women’s education, including greater enrolment in tertiary education when compared to men.
Yet women continue to be under-represented in some of the business functions and sectors that can pave a path to senior leadership.

“At a time when enterprises are competing for skills and talent, leaving women’s potential untapped makes little business sense,” said Maria Paz Anzorreguy, Director of the ILO Bureau for Employers’ Activities.

The report outlines practical measures, including strengthening women’s leadership pipelines, improving access to roles and sectors where women remain under-represented, and using gender metrics and voluntary targets.
It also calls for addressing structural barriers outside the workplace, including unequal care responsibilities, occupational segregation and persistent social norms.
Rosemarie P. Rafael, founder and chairperson of Philippines-based logistics company Airspeed – among three case studies included in the report – shared her perspective with the authors.
“A company with a nurturing culture, with fair recruitment, promotion, and remuneration, will get the best talent, both women and men,” she said.
“And when women know they have a future in the company, they shine.”

articles.title: Esteve hoping for Champions League debut – and Haaland reunion

paras.en: Maxime Esteve interview: RB Leipzig defender on his Erling Haaland reunion after two own goals against Man City

Maxime Esteve is hoping to make his Champions League debut against Manchester City and Erling Haaland, the man he rates as the best striker in the world. In this interview, he discusses working with Vincent Kompany at Burnley and his new life at RB Leipzig…

A reunion with Manchester City brings bad memories for the RB Leipzig defender Maxime Esteve. He scored two own goals at the Etihad Stadium last year. Not that he has advertised this to his new teammates. "Maybe they don't even know," he jokes.

It is an amusing statistic that this time last year, indeed until the final days of November, a dozen games into the Premier League season, Esteve had found the net for City more times than everyone bar Erling Haaland. "This is a secret. You don't have to say!"

The 24-year-old French centre-back left Burnley for Leipzig in the summer and the truth is that he is aching to face City again. He has been on the bench for their opening two Champions League games and is desperate to make his debut in the competition.

"Five years ago, when I was a young kid at Montpellier, my former club, I would have killed to be in this situation now, even if sometimes you do not have the playing time that you want," he explains. "It was always a dream to play for a Champions League club."

Unlucky own goals aside - "and I remember the second was really, really unlucky", Esteve insists - he was brilliant for Burnley. Even in that game against City, his manager Scott Parker made a point of highlighting all his good work in the analysis afterwards.

"I had a meeting on the Monday with him. He told me, 'Max, this is nothing. This is really, really nothing.' Instead, he showed me the good things that I did in the game. Just for the confidence, it was good. It was a bad memory for me at the time but this is football."

Will there be more bad memories after coming up against Haaland again? Esteve acknowledges that Harry Kane has just been honoured with the Ballon d'Or but in his view nobody is better than Haaland. "The best striker I have played against," he says.

"I played just two games against him, but you can see that he is, I think, maybe the best striker in the world. For years, I think he will still be in this position. He is so powerful, so good at heading, so quick. All of the qualities to be a beast." So, how do you stop that?

It is not easy because the temptation is to get tight. "I remember when I played against him, he played with other players, maybe with Rayan Cherki, for example, in the small spaces, so we tried to stay around him." And yet, in a physical battle, it is just as tough.

"You can see as well the habit to sometimes just chip it to the back post and he comes really, really aggressive on you with a big header. He is really good in this box position against the defender, every time in a good position to just finish really good.

"I think he adapts his football against the opponent he is going to play. He did not really touch the ball during the game. He is not that active with the ball. But every time you have to be focused 100 per cent because you know that in one second he can score."

Esteve is unusually thoughtful and you sense that he welcomes detail in his coaching. For example, his video work on opposition strikers extends far beyond their shooting habits. He is fascinating when discussing how their speed dictates his movement.

"It helps you just for the confidence to say, OK, this guy is running at 36 kilometres [per hour] or is he running at 34 [kilometres per hour]? It is quite important because you might have to manage the line a little bit higher or this kind of thing. It is small details."

Maybe it is a product of working with a City legend in Vincent Kompany. The now Bayern Munich coach was in charge at Burnley during Esteve's first season in England. He sees similarities with his current coach, another former City defender in Martin Demichelis.

"It is quite funny. They still want to stay really fit. They play in training. You can see they are quite competitive. They don't want to lose. You can see it. It is still really important for them. They are quite young coaches so they have the new idea of football."

He adds: "We do not play the same football [as Kompany at Leipzig], but in terms of energy, time, work and professionalism, I am going to say they are quite similar. In terms of meetings, they are really perfectionists. They arrive early and they leave really late."

That time-keeping is a feature of life in Germany. "They do not accept anyone being late!" But Esteve is having no problem adjusting. "The facilities, the food, the organisation, everything." The demands are something of a step up after relegation.

"The objective here is to qualify for the Champions League every season." For now, he just wants to play in it. "If I get this opportunity to play, I will be the most happy in the world, to be honest, because you want to realise your dream when you are a kid.

"It is time to integrate myself in the new league, in a new club, new culture as well. For sure, in terms of playing time, I would like to play more, but that is [true] for every player, to be honest. But it is a time for integration and I am here for a long time, I hope.

"I am really happy and really patient. When you come to a bigger club, there is more competition in your position and I totally get that. I just have to wait for my time." That time looks set to come against Man City, of all teams. Just no own goals, please…

articles.title: U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at the end of the year, Trump says
articles.author: Alexander Smith

paras.en: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the United States to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel.
It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant.
Trump said he and Netanyahu “made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” and that the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”

Speaking in a phone interview with “Fox & Friends,” the president said the idea was Netanyahu’s — the Israeli prime minister has previously floated tapering American aid over the next decade. Netanyahu’s office declined to comment Tuesday.

“We’ll help Israel if they need it — you know they’ve been a great ally,” Trump said, adding that the Israeli government was “fine with it because, you know, they have become a very successful country” and “they don’t need” the money.

The president was speaking while voters were heading to the polls for the midterm elections. U.S. military aid to Israel and Israel’s use of American weapons in Gaza and the West Bank has become one of the most contentious issues during the campaign.

The president appeared to acknowledge a political dimension to the decision, saying, “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.”
“I don’t like that because you know it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target,” he said.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump added, referring to Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan progressive Democratic Senate nominee, who has forcefully criticized Israel and U.S. foreign policy during the campaign.

The price of Brent oil slid 3% to $101 in response to Trump’s comments, its lowest level in more than three weeks, as investors and traders viewed the comments as potentially further evidence that the Iran war could be ended without escalation. It ticked back up to $103 as of noon ET.
The initial drop added to oil’s biggest one-day decline in three months Monday, after Trump told NBC News that he was not planning to attack Iran after the midterms.

The U.S. has agreed to give Israel $3.8 billion annually as part of a “memorandum of understanding” between the two countries signed in 2016 under then President Barack Obama. That agreement took effect in October 2018 and specifies $3.3 billion a year in military financing grants and $500 million a year for joint missile defense. It is due to expire in 2028.
Almost all of that money must be spent on purchases from the U.S.
But the total amount is much higher, with American military aid to Israel greatly boosted following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and subsequent Israeli assault on Gaza.

In the two years after October 7, the U.S. spent at least $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to a paper by William D. Hartung, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank based in Washington, D.C.

According to the paper for Brown University’s Costs of War project, some of the $21.7 billion comes in the form of Foreign Military Financing, which is approved by the State Department and implemented by the Pentagon. It pays for weapons that originate in the U.S. and are transferred to other governments.

Another tranche is Offshore Procurement, in which U.S. funds are given to Israel for it to bolster its own military. Other funds are used to replenish U.S. weapons stocks supplied to Israel, and “special funding” for ammunition and arms production capacity, the paper said.

“U.S. arms have been central to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and Israel Police operations in Gaza, the West Bank, and beyond,” the study said, including “Israel’s entire inventory of combat capable aircraft,” which as of the study’s publication in October last year was 75 F-15s, 196 F-16s, and 39 F-35s.

In January, the Netanyahu said that he hoped to “taper off” American military aid over the next decade. On Tuesday, Trump said that halting the money by the end of this year was the Israeli prime minister’s idea.

“Can I be honest with you? He brought it up,” Trump added. “He said: ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid,’ because he understands that this is one of their points of contention.”
Trump and Netanyahu launched the war on Iran earlier this year, and munitions in the U.S. have been increasingly depleted as a result.
Trump’s comments were seized upon by Netanyahu’s domestic political opponents.

“The fact that the defense establishment — along with the citizens of Israel — learned of a shift in the strategic relationship through the media, demonstrates just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a real danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals who previously served as IDF Chief of Staff.

“He can no longer be trusted, and he must be replaced,” added Eisenkot, who has head of the Yashar party has received backing from Netanyahu’s other opponents to replace him as prime minister following inconclusive elections last month.
Yair Golan, head of the left-wing Democrats party, added that “the cessation of American aid deals a severe blow to Israel’s security and the quality of life in the country.”

“At a time when Israel’s defense expenditures have reached massive proportions, when Israel needs to replenish its stocks of offensive weaponry, and when air defense capabilities have been eroded following such a prolonged war,” Golan added. “Netanyahu has notched yet another colossal failure to his name.”
